docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Cliff Detection Subsystem is designed to prevent the robot from driving off elevated surfaces. It uses two TCRT5000 reflective infrared sensors connected to a Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano.

The microcontroller monitors reflected infrared light from the ground and communicates potential cliff hazards to the master controller.

docs.title: Power Source
docs.text:
• 3S Li-ion battery (9–12.6 V) or 9 V bench adapter
  • J1 barrel jack
  • 750 mA fuse (proposed)
  • LM2940CT-5.0 voltage regulator
  • Regulated 5 V power supply
  • USB connection for programming and debugging

The Curiosity Nano's external power connection must be configured according to Microchip's hardware requirements.

docs.title: Sensors
docs.text:
The subsystem uses two TCRT5000 reflective infrared sensors, positioned on the left and right sides of the robot.

Each sensor contains an infrared LED and phototransistor. The LED emits infrared light toward the ground, while the phototransistor detects reflected light.

The sensor outputs are read through the Curiosity Nano's analog-to-digital converter.

docs.title: Team Interfaces
docs.text:
The subsystem communicates with the master controller through Connector 4 using UART2.

The ribbon cable carries UART transmit, receive, and common ground connections. Exact connector pin assignments must be confirmed with the team.

docs.title: Functional Description
docs.text:
Power enters the subsystem through the J1 barrel jack and passes through fuse protection and a 5 V voltage regulator.

The two TCRT5000 sensors continuously monitor reflected infrared light from the ground.

The Curiosity Nano reads the sensor signals through RA0 and RA1 and compares them against calibrated thresholds.

When either sensor detects a possible loss of ground, the Curiosity Nano sends a cliff warning to the master controller through UART2.

The master controller can then command the motor subsystem to stop or change direction.

docs.title: Part 1: Component Comparison
docs.text: The purpose of the Cliff Detection subsystem is to detect when the robot approaches an edge or drop-off. Three sensors were considered based on cost, sensing capabilities, electrical requirements, and integration with the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

docs.title: 1. TCRT5000 Infrared Reflective Sensor
docs.text:
Price: $1.63

Pros: - Low-cost and readily available. - Compact design with an infrared emitter and phototransistor. - Can detect changes in reflected infrared light. - Simple analog interface with the PIC18F57Q43.

Cons: - Reflectivity changes with floor color and material. - Requires external resistors and signal conditioning. - Sensitive to sensor mounting height and alignment. - Does not directly measure distance.

View TCRT5000 on DigiKey

docs.title: 2. VL6180X-SATEL Time-of-Flight Sensor
docs.text:
Price: $22.70 (assignment reference)

Pros: - Measures physical distance rather than reflected light intensity. - Less affected by floor color. - Provides precise distance measurements. - Compact optical sensor.

Cons: - Higher cost than the TCRT5000. - Requires I2C communication. - More complex software integration. - Measurement timing must be considered.

View VL6180X-SATEL on DigiKey

docs.title: 3. VL53L0CXV0DH/1 Time-of-Flight Sensor
docs.text:
Price: $4.63 (assignment reference)

Pros: - Measures physical distance using time-of-flight technology. - Less dependent on surface reflectivity. - Compact footprint. - Supports precise distance threshold detection.

Cons: - Requires low-voltage power and compatible logic levels. - Uses I2C communication. - Requires additional software configuration. - Surface-mount package complicates assembly.

View VL53L0CXV0DH/1 on DigiKey

docs.title: Part 2A: Electrical Requirements
docs.text:
The following values were recorded in the initial component comparison.

Component Voltage Current Listed PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano 3.3V / 5.0V 50 mA TCRT5000 5.0V 60 mA VL6180X-SATEL 2.8V–5.0V 19 mA VL53L0CXV0DH/1 2.8V–3.3V 19 mA

Important: The TCRT5000's 60 mA value is the infrared LED's absolute maximum continuous forward current, not its required operating current.

The sensor contains two electrically separate components: 1. Infrared LED — requires a current-limiting resistor. 2. Phototransistor — requires a sensing circuit to produce a usable output voltage.

docs.title: Selected Component: TCRT5000
docs.text:
The TCRT5000 was selected for the Cliff Detection subsystem because of its low cost, compact size, and relatively simple electrical interface.

The sensor uses an infrared LED to illuminate the floor and a phototransistor to detect reflected infrared light.

When the robot travels over a reflective surface, infrared light returns to the phototransistor. When the robot approaches an edge, the amount of reflected light decreases. The PIC18F57Q43 can monitor this change and determine whether a possible cliff is present.

Compared with the VL6180X-SATEL and VL53L0CXV0DH/1, the TCRT5000 does not require I2C communication. This simplifies integration with the microcontroller.

The primary disadvantage is sensitivity to different floor materials and colors. Testing and calibration will be required to establish reliable detection thresholds.

docs.title: Integration Plan
docs.text:
1. Supply the infrared LED through a current-limiting resistor.
  2. Connect the phototransistor to an appropriate sensing circuit.
  3. Connect the sensing circuit output to a PIC18F57Q43 ADC input.
  4. Calibrate the reflected-light threshold.
  5. Send a cliff detection signal to the robot's control system when the threshold is crossed.
